operative_text.controlling:
3.3(1)   The appropriate judicial centre for the purpose of these
rules is
(a) the closest judicial centre, by road, to the Alberta
residences or Alberta places of business of all the parties,
or
(b) if a single judicial centre cannot be determined under
clause (a), the judicial centre that is, by road, the closest to
the Alberta residence or Alberta place of business of one
of the parties, that party being selected by the party
starting the action.
(2)  If a party carries on business in more than one Alberta location,
the place of business in Alberta of that party for the purpose of this
rule is the place of business that is nearest to the location at which
the matters in issue in the action arose or were transacted.
(3)  Despite subrules (1) and (2), the parties may agree on a judicial
centre in which to start and carry on the action, in which case the
judicial centre agreed on by the parties is the appropriate judicial
centre unless the Court otherwise orders.

BOOK_A.commentary:
Rule 3.3 sets out how to determine the appropriate judicial centre in which to commence and

carry on, or to transfer, an action.On when a suit once in the appropriate centre now should be moved to another, see R.3.5 and notes. The Rules were heavily amended in 1996, and pre-1996 cases giving the plaintiff's choice great weight are no longer law, but the new 2010 Rules make no real change to the 1996 Rules. No longer do the odd boundaries of judicialdistrictsgovern;now the test is distance to judicial

*centresby usual methods of travel. The Rules are designed to prevent a plaintiff's picking a venue for the suit which has no connection at all with the location of either party. If the relevant parties to the lawsuit clearly are in or close to one judicial centre, that is where the plaintiff must start the lawsuit.The defendants

have a right to have it moved there if it was not started there.That the non-resident plaintiff wants to run all its foreclosure actions in one judicial centre and use one counsel, is not enough to depart from the Rule. Calgary cannot be the proper judicial centre if both parties reside in Edmonton, and the court should transfer the suit under R.3.5, if R.3.3 was not complied with;the place in R. 3.3 is presumed correct.

BOOK_B.title: Determining the appropriate judicial centre

commentary.text: Rule 3.3 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.3. 1. Old Cases Apply to R. 3.3(2) In 325303 Alberta Ltd. v. Prime Property Management, 2011 ABQB 817, 2011 CarswellAlta 2313, 531 A.R. 204, there was an application under R. 3.3(2) to transfer the action from Edmonton to the Judicial Centre to Grande Prairie. Justice Michalyshyn said, at paragraph 5: 5 Rule 3.3(2) repeats previous Rule 6.1(2)(d) virtually verbatim. And for the purpose of what I have to decide, the balance of changes from the previous rules to the whole of Rule 3.3 (and for that matter Rule 3.5 which is similar to previous Rule 12) are of no consequence. As such, on the face of it cases decided under previous Rules 6.1 and 237 are relevant to my consideration of Rule 3.3(2) in particular. In Apache Canada Ltd. v. Johnson, 2005 ABCA 71, 2005 CarswellAlta 190, 363 A.R. 100, Fruman J.A. discussed previous Rule 6.1(2). At pp. 102-103, her Ladyship said: Rule 6.1 changed the procedure for determining where an action is to be instituted. Essentially, the rule directs a plaintiff to commence its legal action in the closest judicial centre as determined under R. 6.1(2) … Notwithstanding the other rules, the parties may agree in writing to a particular judicial district. In addition, a chambers judge may select the judicial district that is most appropriate (R. 6.1(3)). See also R. 12. However, a judicial district selected by a plaintiff in accordance with R. 6.1(2) will not be set aside lightly. The defendant must show the balance of convenience clearly favours transferring the action to another judicial district. The parties agree that Apache carries on business in Calgary, where its regional office is located. The appellants contend Apache also carries on business in Provost, where Apache has a gas plant and a field office with 50 employees and where many interactions between the appellants and Apache relating to the lawsuit took place. The appellants say that Provost is closer than Calgary to the location at which the matters in question in the action—the wrongful conversion of gas—arose. They therefore submit R. 6.1(2)(a) and (d) apply and Wetaskiwin is the appropriate judicial district. The term “carries on business” is not defined in the Alberta Rules of Court. The term appears in many statutes and its meaning is coloured by the legislative context. It is therefore inappropriate to simply import a definition from another statute. Instead, it is necessary to look at the purpose of R. 6.1, which is to make a lawsuit more convenient and fair to all parties. See Lim et al. v. Young et al. (2004), 360 A.R. 277, 2004 ABQB 489. This is done by requiring a significant connection between the parties and the judicial district in which the action is commenced. In order to establish whether a significant connection exists in a particular case, it is necessary to examine the particular structure of the corporation's operations, the nature of and issues in the lawsuit, and the relationship between the parties in respect of those issues. Such examinations are fact specific. In this case, the chambers judge stated that a field operation was not what was intended by R. 6.1. In doing so, he did not consider the appropriate contextual factors, which was an error of law. In Odland v. Odland, 2017 ABCA 397, 2017 CarswellAlta 2490, 63 Alta. L.R. (6th) 55, 12 C.P.C. (8th) 24, the Court said: 1 Once a plaintiff commences an action in a particular judicial centre and the defendant wishes to transfer the action to another judicial centre on the basis that the plaintiff's choice was inappropriate, who bears the onus to establish that the plaintiff's choice of venue was reasonable? We conclude that the onus is on the defendant if the plaintiff's selection of judicial centre was in compliance with rule 3.3. However, if the plaintiff's selection of judicial centre did not comply with rule 3.3, the plaintiff has the onus of proving the choice was reasonable. … 7 The leading case under the now-repealed Rules on the appropriate judicial centre in which to commence an action is Apache Canada Ltd v Johnson, 2005 ABCA 71, 363 AR 100. The Apache Canada test must be modified to conform to rule 3.3, which governs. More specifically: i. A statement of claim must be filed in the judicial centre that is closest to the Alberta residences or places of business of all parties: r 3.3(1)(a). ii. If a single judicial centre cannot be so determined, the statement of claim must be filed in the judicial centre that is closest by road to the Alberta residence or place of business of one of the parties, as selected by the party starting the action: r 3.3(1)(b). iii. If there is more than one place of business in Alberta, the place of business for the purposes of this rule is the one nearest the location where the matters in the action arose or were transacted: r 3.3(2). iv. The parties may otherwise agree on a judicial centre to start and carry on the action: r 3.3(3). 8 The purpose of the repealed rule was to make a lawsuit “convenient and fair to all parties”: Apache Canada at para 7. That is also the purpose of rule 3.3. 9 The plaintiff submits that she has the discretion to select the judicial centre as long as her choice is not “arbitrary or capricious”, citing Wade Investment Ltd v Hat Travel Ltd (1979), 21 AR 454, 1979 CarswellAlta 433 (WL Can) (QB). 10 Apache and cases since rejected this approach: Apache Canada at paras 3-4; 325303 Alberta Ltd v Prime Property Management, 2011 ABQB 817 at paras 14-15, 531 AR 204. 11 Rule 3.3 requires that when there is no single closest judicial centre to the Alberta residences of all the parties, the plaintiff must select the closest judicial centre to the residence of one of them: r 3.3(1)(a) and (b), with emphasis. 12 The plaintiff's selection of Calgary is not a judicial centre contemplated by rule 3.3 because neither party resides in Calgary. 13 The court has the discretion to transfer the action if the plaintiff's selection of judicial centre was incorrect: r 3.5; 325303 Alberta Ltd at paras 21-22. Since both parties' Alberta residences are in the judicial centre of Edmonton, that is the proper judicial centre.

BOOK_C.title: Determining the appropriate judicial centre

commentary.text: Rule 3.3 provides guidance to determine which judicial centre is the most appropriate to start a legal action. It has nothing to do with determining the appropriate forum in the face of competing jurisdictions. Parties can agree on a judicial centre. If an agreement cannot be reached, a party may apply to court to have an action moved from one judicial centre to another. Also, the justices of the Court of King’s Bench have jurisdiction over the entirety of the province and can, on occasion, make orders in one judicial centre that affect an action filed in another.

Rule text, amendment note and (empty) information notes agree with the official 3.3 and Book A.
